questions.question: A student wants to compute a $4\times4$ determinant by copying the first columns and drawing diagonals as in Sarrus' rule. What is the main problem?
options: Sarrus needs the first three columns copied, not just two.
Sarrus' diagonal shortcut works only for $3\times3$ determinants.
The shortcut gives the right terms but with the wrong signs.
The shortcut works only if the $4\times4$ matrix is symmetric.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\1&2&3\\0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$, what should Sarrus' rule give?
In Sarrus' rule for $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{pmatrix}$, which product is one of the positive products?
options: $aei$
$ceg$
$afh$
$bdi$

questions.question: When comparing Sarrus' rule with cofactor expansion for a $3\times3$ determinant, what is true?
options: Sarrus' rule changes the value when rows are swapped.
Sarrus' rule computes the trace instead.
Cofactor expansion only works for diagonal matrices.
They give the same determinant, organised differently

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&1\\3&-1&4\\5&0&2\end{pmatrix}$, what determinant is obtained by Sarrus' rule?

Sarrus' rule for a $3\times3$ matrix $\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})$ copies the first two columns to the right and uses the products along three falling and three rising diagonals. Which of these products is not one of the six Sarrus products?

For a $3\times3$ matrix $\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})$, Sarrus' rule adds the product $a_{12}a_{23}a_{31}$. In the cofactor expansion of $\det\boldsymbol{A}$ along the first row, the entry $a_{12}$ carries the cofactor sign $-$. Why do both methods still give this product with a plus sign?
options: Only the totals of the two methods agree; individual terms may differ in sign.
The cofactor sign at position $(1,2)$ is in fact $+$, so the $a_{12}$ term is added.
The product lies on a rising diagonal, and rising diagonal products are added.
The minor of $a_{12}$ contributes $-a_{23}a_{31}$, and this sign cancels the cofactor sign.
